newsitem.title: UK: Britain plans tough anti-stalking laws.
newsitem.headline: Britain plans tough anti-stalking laws.

text.p: Britain announced tough measures on Friday to curb so-called stalkers after a series of high-profile cases including the arrest of a German doctor who pursued Princess Diana for months.
Under the proposals, persistent stalkers -- people who obsessively follow and harrass their victims -- could face up to five years in prison or an unlimited fine.
Their victims can ask police for protection if the stalker has used intimidating words or behaviour on just two occasions.
"These laws would be a double deterrent," said Home Office (interior ministry) minister David Maclean.
"The new criminal offences would punish stalkers for the harm they have already caused, and give the police the power to intervene at an early stage," he said.
The government expects to the proposals to become law next spring.
Offences covered under the act could included repeated telephone calls or sending of flowers to an unwilling recipient.
The government had come under pressure to introduce new measures after a spate of highly-publicised stalking cases.

In July, a male stalker received a suspended sentence after terrorising a 13-year-old girl for 10 months and, last month, a man was found guilty of causing grievous bodily harm to a dental nurse he subjected to an eight month campaign of intimidation in which police recorded 200 incidents.
Princess Diana and her former sister-in-law Princess Anne have both been victims of stalkers.
Klaus Wagner, a German doctor who sparked security scares by turning up bearing placards at Diana's private and public engagements, was sent to a mental hospital for 28 days in March.
Another man accused of stalking Princess Anne was freed in January after a judge ruled that he posed no threat to Queen Elizabeth's only daughter although he had followed her relentlessly.

An opposition Labour member of parliament, Janet Anderson, who tried unsuccessfully to push an anti-stalking bill through parliament in May says about 3,000 Britons, mainly women, are victims of stalkers every year.
